expansion:
A is correct. This presentation is central retinal artery occlusion: sudden profound painless monocular visual loss with retinal whitening and a cherry-red macular spot. The acute-visual-loss lecture presents the same combination and identifies it as “Central Retinal Artery Occlusion” (L31,32, slide 4–9). In its case, the swinging-flashlight test “confirms a right relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil)” (L31,32, slide 6). Here, the affected eye is the left eye, so the defect is ipsilateral: a left RAPD. The pupil dilates paradoxically as the light is swung to that eye because the afferent light signal is relatively weaker; the pupil-and-visual-pathway lecture illustrates that, with light on the defective eye, “the pupils actually dilate as the torch swings across to it” (L22, slide 6). The retinal vascular lecture also lists CRAO with “APD - marked,” “Retinal whitening,” and “‘Cherry-red spot’ at macula” (L19.2, page 26).

B is wrong because an RAPD is assigned to the eye with the impaired afferent retinal/optic-nerve input, not to the fellow eye. The vignette specifically says that illumination of the left eye causes dilation, localising the relative afferent defect to the left eye.

C is wrong because Argyll Robertson pupil is a different pupil abnormality. The lecture describes “Small pupils” and “Light Near dissociation,” associated with affection of the pretectal area, neurosyphilis, DM, alcoholism, and encephalitis (L22, slide 8). It does not describe the unilateral swinging-flashlight finding in this case.

D is wrong because Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon is an eyelid synkinesis, not an afferent pupillary defect. The course names “Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome” as an indication for frontalis brow suspension (L5, slide 9), whereas it separately calls RAPD the “Marcus Gunn Pupil” (L31,32, slide 6).
objective: Identify paradoxical dilation on swinging-flashlight testing as an ipsilateral relative afferent pupillary defect.
